prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform a lumbar puncture while the left parietal lesion causes midline shift and papilloedema
Do not start corticosteroids before tissue has been obtained, except dexamethasone for impending herniation after neurosurgical discussion
Do not resect the lesion or start radiotherapy or chemotherapy on the imaging appearance or the family history alone
Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics
Do not start teriflunomide in a woman of child-bearing potential without effective contraception (teratogenic, long elimination half-life)
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance treatment for MS: they do not prevent relapses or disability and cause cumulative harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS by the 2024 McDonald criteria, naming the regions that give DIS and, where needed, what gives DIT or positive CSF (here periventricular and spinal cord, with DIT from the enhancing tumefactive lesion alongside non-enhancing lesions, after histology has excluded neoplasm).

Withhold corticosteroids until neurosurgical stereotactic biopsy of the left parietal lesion has been obtained, because steroids can make lymphoma non-diagnostic; dexamethasone only for impending herniation and after neurosurgical discussion.
Manage the raised intracranial pressure: head of bed at 30 degrees, frequent neurological observations, osmotherapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline) for deterioration, and urgent neurosurgical review.

Once histology shows demyelination, give IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days with a proton pump inhibitor (she takes ibuprofen) and glucose monitoring; plasma exchange if the response is inadequate.

Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (a tumefactive enhancing lesion with mass effect: a high-efficacy therapy is reasonable), after discussing pregnancy plans and contraception.

Before starting disease-modifying therapy, screen HBsAg, anti-HBc, HCV, HIV (done) and VZV IgG, add anti-JCV antibodies if natalizumab is considered, and give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before starting.

avoided_actions.rationale: A 4.1 cm left parietal mass with 6 mm midline shift and bilateral papilloedema makes lumbar puncture unsafe because of the risk of herniation.
No seizure or altered awareness; an EEG would not help characterise the lesion or change management.
Afebrile with no murmur or embolic pattern: no cardiac source question for a single tumefactive lesion.
No palpitations, syncope or rhythm question.
Brain FDG-PET would not remove the need for tissue; the biopsy answers the question.

differential.key_features: Raised by a periventricular-extending enhancing lesion; the steroid-free biopsy shows active demyelination with only scattered reactive CD20-positive B cells and no atypical lymphoid infiltrate; HIV negative.

Raised by mass effect, raised choline on spectroscopy and the father's glioblastoma; the biopsy shows demyelination with reactive astrocytes and no atypical glial cells, mitoses, microvascular proliferation or necrosis; open ring and rim rCBV 1.4 also argue against it.
Afebrile with normal CRP and ESR; restricted diffusion at the leading edge rather than in the core; histology shows no organisms or suppuration.
No known primary; open ring with an additional ovoid periventricular lesion and a cord lesion; histology without malignant cells.
AQP4-IgG negative by cell-based assay; short dorsal C3-C4 lesion; no optic neuritis or area postrema syndrome.
MOG-IgG negative by cell-based assay; no optic neuritis or ADEM-like multifocal disease.
No encephalopathy and no preceding infection or vaccination; a non-enhancing periventricular lesion and a non-enhancing cord lesion point to lesions of different age.

key_clinical_evidence: One week of headache and two days of progressive right hemiparesis with right hyperreflexia, a right Babinski sign and bilateral papilloedema, from a 4.1 cm left parietal lesion with open-ring enhancement facing the cortex, leading-edge restricted diffusion, oedema and 6 mm midline shift.
DIS: 2 of 5 regions: periventricular (right periventricular ovoid lesion), spinal cord (dorsal C3-C4, 12 mm).
DIT: simultaneous enhancing (left parietal) and non-enhancing (right periventricular, C3-C4) lesions on the same examination.
Stereotactic biopsy: active demyelination with myelin-laden macrophages, perivascular T cells and relative axonal preservation; no atypical lymphoid or glial cells.
AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG negative by cell-based assay, with a short dorsal cord lesion: against NMOSD and MOGAD.
Perfusion (rim rCBV 1.4) and spectroscopy (raised choline, lactate) do not separate demyelination from tumour here, and the midline shift with papilloedema makes lumbar puncture unsafe.
The father's glioblastoma is a distractor: it does not change the imaging or the histology.

metadata.difficulty_description: A 4.1 cm enhancing left parietal lesion with mass effect, midline shift and papilloedema mimics high-grade glioma, and the father's glioblastoma adds a distractor. Lumbar puncture is unsafe and perfusion and spectroscopy are indeterminate, so the agent must recognise the open-ring and leading-edge diffusion features, find the second-region lesions (right periventricular, C3-C4 cord), and obtain tissue before corticosteroids.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Tumefactive demyelinating lesion with mass effect: the agent must avoid lumbar puncture, exclude lymphoma and glioma by biopsy before steroids, exclude NMOSD/MOGAD by serum CBA, and still apply the McDonald criteria (2 regions plus MRI DIT).

patient.history_present_illness: A 28-year-old previously healthy right-handed Hispanic woman presents to the emergency department with a one-week history of progressively worsening headache and two days of progressive right-sided weakness, with nausea and one episode of vomiting. The headache began a week ago as a mild holocephalic ache and has become severe (8/10), worse in the morning, with nausea and photophobia. Two days ago, on awakening, she noticed difficulty gripping her coffee mug with her right hand. Since yesterday she has had difficulty walking because of weakness in her right leg, prompting her partner to bring her to the emergency department. She denies any preceding febrile illness, recent travel, insect bites, or trauma. She has no prior history of neurological symptoms, seizures, or similar episodes. She was seen by her primary care physician 6 months ago for a routine physical and was in good health. Of note, her father was diagnosed with glioblastoma at age 52 and passed away two years ago, which is causing her significant anxiety about the possibility of a brain tumor. She denies any recent weight loss, night sweats, or changes in appetite. She reports no visual changes, speech difficulties, or sensory symptoms. She has been taking combined oral contraceptives for the past 3 years without complications.
